query: For AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock intended for additively manufactured miniature components, what single intervention could overcome the residual thermal stresses, degraded mechanical properties, and processing complexity associated with mainstream metallic additive-manufacturing regimes? Formulate one hypothesis that specifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to components made under conventional high-thermal-load additive-manufacturing conditions, states the applicable processing window, geometry, and test conditions, identifies supporting prior evidence, and describes a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Integrating an in-situ, low‐temperature annealing step (operating at or below 700 °C) during the laser powder-bed fusion processing of AlCrFeNiSi powder will reduce residual thermal stresses, refine the microstructure, and improve mechanical properties compared to components produced under conventional high-thermal-load regimes.
generation.material_initial_state: Pre-alloyed AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock prepared for additive manufacturing.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled, low-temperature annealing step between laser passes during the PBF-LB process.
generation.conditions: Manufacture miniature components with a layer thickness of 20–50 µm using PBF-LB; incorporate a dwell period between layers to maintain the build temperature at or below 700 °C. Evaluate components under ambient and cryogenic test conditions, ensuring the geometry (miniature, thin-walled structures) is consistent across samples.
generation.structural_mediator: The temporary annealing reduces dislocation density and mitigates grain size variation across the build height.
generation.mechanism: The low-temperature annealing relieves residual stresses by allowing limited diffusion and dislocation rearrangement without triggering full recrystallization, thereby producing a more uniform microstructure and preserving mechanical integrity.
generation.predicted_outcome: Components fabricated with the in-situ annealing step will exhibit lower residual stresses, a more homogeneous microstructure with refined grains, enhanced ductility, and yield strength that is comparable or superior to those produced by conventional high-energy deposition regimes.
generation.baseline: Components produced via conventional high-thermal-load PBF-LB without in-situ annealing, which typically suffer from residual stress buildup, heterogeneous microstructures over the build height, and degraded mechanical performance.
generation.boundary: This intervention is expected to be effective for miniature, additively manufactured components using AlCrFeNiSi; its efficacy for larger-scale builds or other alloy systems remains to be determined.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal dwell time and precise temperature control required to balance stress relief with preservation of layer adhesion are not fully established. Additionally, scalability and throughput impact of the in-situ annealing step require further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of miniature AlCrFeNiSi components using PBF-LB under identical overall processing conditions. One set employs the integrated low-temperature annealing step (dwell at ≤700 °C between layers), while the control set uses conventional high-thermal-load deposition without intermediate annealing.
measurements: Residual stress measurements via X-ray diffraction
Microstructural analysis using SEM/EBSD to assess grain size and dislocation density
Mechanical testing (tensile tests) to measure yield strength and ductility
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the components with the in-situ annealing step do not show statistically significant reductions in residual stress and improvements in microstructural homogeneity and mechanical properties compared to the control group, the hypothesis is falsified.

## Abstract
Directed energy deposition (DED), as an additive manufacturing technology, has shown unique advantages in multi-material additive manufacturing and remanufacturing. In this study, two types in-situ alloyed CrCoNi medium entropy alloys that have thin-walled structures with different thicknesses (T1 and T2) were manufactured by the DED process, and the mechanisms of differences in relative density, microstructure, and mechanical properties at different heights were systematically analyzed. In terms of microstructure, the T1 and T2 samples along the building direction exhibit significant differences in crystallographic orientation, grain size, and dislocation density, which are related to the local temperature gradient differences caused by the scanning path and heat accumulation. In terms of mechanical properties at different heights of the two types of thin-walled structures, the yield strength is higher but the elongation is lower at the bottom position of sample, while the yield strength is lower but the elongation is higher at the middle and top positions. ## Abstract
Eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs) exhibit excellent casting properties and comprehensive mechanical performance, making them suitable for fabricating spatial engineering components using additive manufacturing techniques. However, the rapid solidification process also leads to increased internal stress and reduced structural stability in the components. Therefore, this study focuses on the AlFeCoCrNi2.1 EHEA as the research subject, utilizing laser additive manufacturing to fabricate components and systematically investigating the influence of heat treatment processes on the microstructure and mechanical properties of the components. The research demonstrates that low-temperature heat treatment (700 °C and below) acts as a stress relief-annealing process for the components. The yield strength decreased from 1003.2 MPa to 742.1 MPa. At 900 °C heat treatment, the constraining effect between recrystallized grains and surrounding grains outweighs the dislocation release effect caused by recrystallization, resulting in an increase in dislocation density. Available technologies range from multi-step processes, utilizing binding media, followed by debinding and sintering steps, to single-step technologies, which completely melt the feedstock [,,]. Thus, multi-step processes rely on solid-state sintering to achieve the microstructure of the part, analogous to traditional powder metallurgy, whereas single-step processes generate a solidification microstructure while simultaneously shaping the part.
A melting metallurgical approach becomes difficult when elements with very different melting and evaporation points are present in the alloy, thus, complicating the processability via single-step AM processes. The fabrication of metals in single-step AM processes occurs predominantly through full melting of the feedstock and as such, incorporates the melting metallurgical approach []. In addition, segregations can pose a challenge in cases with slow solidification rates. However, single-step processes can also be beneficial, since the dynamic flows in the melt pool can help to achieve a homogeneous mixture of alloying elements, especially in the absence of pre-alloyed powders.
